content.content:
# Families, forms, materials and textures

Moved from the root `CLAUDE.md`, word for word: the root keeps the rules and the map, and this file is read when the area is touched.

A family (`Model::families`, `family.rs`) is parameters, types that set them and forms in its own axes: x along a
component's angle, y to its left, z up from its base; a form is a profile in a sketch plane (`xy` swept up, `xz` along y,
`yz` along x), its sizes numbers or formulas, or triangles as a file brings them. A component places a type;
`Model::component_pieces` are its forms where it stands. Plans draw them from above, a form's edges hidden under a higher
form of the same component; sections show them beyond their line and never cut them (a `Solid::Mesh` is cut only where its `cut`
says, as a round run's tube is); the
3D view takes a form's triangles that share an edge and turn under 20° there as one curved surface, so a curve draws no
edge between its facets (`view3d::facets`) and shades smoothly across them, each corner lit by the angle-weighted mean of
its own surface's normals there, so a crease keeps its step (`corner_normals`); IFC writes each form as a closed face set,
triangles turned out, and reads one family per family name the file gives.

A form is swept, or with an `axis` turned about it (`family::revolve`: `from` to `to` degrees, 32 steps to a turn, the profile to
one side of the axis); a `void` cuts the solid forms listed before it (`csg::subtract`: convex polygons in binary space
partitions, built and walked with a worklist rather than recursion and bounded by a `Meter`, so a hostile shape ends in an error;
a cut piece keeps its uncut outline in plan). A family of category `door` or `window` is hosted: its `Width` and `Height` (English
names, whatever the project's language) size the wall's opening, `Sill Height` is a window's default sill, its forms are drawn in
the opening's axes (x along the wall from the middle of the opening, y across it from the wall's middle plane and + toward its
exterior, z up from the sill) and its formulas read `Wall Thickness`; its `symbols` also draw in plan (a door's swing). Its `connectors` say what an electrical device draws ([structure and MEP](structure-and-mep.md)); a family file keeps them. An
`Opening` holds a `family`, or none (one of the project's own types): `Model::opening_dims` gives its size either way
(`opening_type` returns it by value), its flips are mirrors (`opening_local`), and `Element::family()` is the one way to ask what
family a component or an opening is of. Sections show a family opening's forms beyond their line and never cut them.
How a door or a window opens is its family's `operation` (`model::Operation`: swing, double-swing, sliding, double-sliding,
folding, fixed), or for one of the project's own types the type's (`OpeningType::operation`); none, a door swings. IFC writes
it as the door's `OperationType` (`Operation::ifc_door`, its side from `flip_hand`: `SLIDING_TO_RIGHT`) and a window's
`PartitioningType` (two leaves, `DOUBLE_PANEL_VERTICAL`); the import reads a door's back, or its `IfcDoorType`'s (IFC4) or
`IfcDoorStyle`'s (IFC2x3), onto the type it makes. Schedules have it as the `Operation` field, in the project's language. A
window's panel operation (`IfcWindowPanelProperties`, a sliding sash) needs an `IfcWindowType`, which the export doesn't write yet.
A material's `texture` (`texture.rs`) is a pattern drawn in code or a picture of `Model::images` (a PNG or JPEG comes in, is kept
as a PNG of at most 1024 px, its header checked before the decoder makes room for it), laid on a face at its `size` in mm by the
face's own axes (`view3d::basis`: across is level, up goes up it, east and north where it lies flat), sampled per pixel from the
depth buffer, in the 3D view alone, from a mip chain. A triangle carries a skin (`view3d::skin`): in its low 24 bits a texture id (one more than its material's place in the
library), in its high 8 its material's `transparency`; `Scene::new` resolves the textures. A material's `transparency` (percent,
0 to 100, 0 opaque and not written, the starter Glass 70) is how see-through the 3D view draws what is made of it, with no view
override: a layer's skin wins over its element's, paint gives a face its own, and a family-less window's glass takes the Glass
material's. IFC carries it in `IFCSURFACESTYLESHADING`'s second argument (0 opaque to 1 clear, `$` for opaque), read back from a
shading or a rendering. Only the nearest see-through surface is blended, so a glass wall's far face and stacked glass don't
accumulate; plans and sections ignore it. Paint (`paint.rs`) is `{face: material}` in an element's `params` under `Paint`, a reserved
name: a triangle's face is read from its winding, so every solid emits triangles turned out (`Solid::tris`, `prism`), and
`Image::face` says which face a pixel is on. Favorites (`favorites.rs`) are a file of the user's own (`default_path`:
`BIMCRAFT_FAVORITES`, else the configuration folder) with materials and their pictures, families and their materials; they change
a project only through the `favorite` command (`load` never overwrites without `replace`). The desktop's Family Editor
(`editor.rs`) edits text (`FormText`, `ParamText`, ...) and changes the project's family only through a `family` command; its
preview is a scratch `Session` of its own, and it says what's wrong inside the window (the status box, over the view's corner, would lie on its
buttons).

A type of a category or of a family is renamed with `rename_type` (`Model::move_entry` moves it in its map, and `rename_entry` the
library entry and every reference `Model::lib_refs_mut` visits, so it keeps its GUID). A type or a family goes with `delete_type` (one entry, refused while an element uses it, and for the last type of a category or of a family: a
tool needs one to place) and `purge` (every entry of the kinds asked that nothing uses). Use is what `Model::lib_refs_mut` visits, the one place
that names every reference to a library entry: `Model::library_uses` counts them on a copy of the model, `Model::unused_entries` is one pass of
what purge takes out (each category keeps its default's type, else its first; a family that goes takes its types), the command repeats it
for what a pass frees (a family's material, a type's), at most 16 times, on a copy that becomes the model only when it isn't a `dry_run`.
`Model::remove_entry` is the single place that knows where each kind lives. The desktop's Purge Unused window (`purge.rs`) lists a dry run
for the kinds checked and runs the same; the Project Browser's Families lists the system types and has the right-click Delete.

The `family` command works out the whole change before the model is touched (`commands.rs::family`), so reading one costs no undo step
and a family `Model::check` would refuse never enters it. `family {name}` alone reads: the definition with every form's and symbol's `id`
and `GUID`, each type's `values` worked out, and `warnings` — no `model_mut()`, no file. Without `name` it lists the project's families
with their category and how much of each there is; `save` still writes one to a file. `dry_run: true` builds the change it's given
locally and replies `ok`, `warnings`, `changes` (parameters and types added, taken away and changed; forms and symbols replaced, patched
and deleted by id; the rename) instead of doing it; a refusal comes back as an error exactly as it would without it, carrying every error
and warning found, not only the first. One form or symbol is patched by its `id` or `guid` (`form`/`symbol`: its fields merged over what
that one holds, a `null` taking one away, its place, id and GUID kept; `delete_form`/`delete_symbol` to take it away), where `forms` and
`symbols` still replace whole lists — `keep_parts` binds by place, so patching is what leaves the other parts' ids alone. Validation is
`family/validate.rs` (`Family::problems`): every formula read at once (`names`, unknown parameters besides a hosted family's
`Wall Thickness`, syntax errors with the character they stop at), then `Family::check`, plus geometry warnings best worked out around
what doesn't build — a void reaching no solid before it, a form wholly outside its opening, one thicker than its wall, a door's or
window's plan with no symbols — each aggregated as `(in type …)`. `Family::shapes` gives each form's box before any void cuts it, from
the same `solid` `build` uses. `render {family, type, mode}` draws a family on its own: a `Session::new()` of its own holding the
project's materials and images, a wall of `wall_thickness` mm for a hosted family (a floor of its own footprint otherwise) with the type
in it, then `render_view` on that model — `3d`, `plan` (what its symbols draw) or `elevation` (front-on) — and the project keeps no
element and no undo step from it, the way the Family Editor's own preview already worked (`editor.rs::scratch`).


## Plan symbols

A family's `symbols`, of any category, are what its plan draws besides its forms, in its own axes: each is exactly one of a
`line` (up to `MAX_PROFILE` points), an `arc`, a `text` or a `dot`, with `visible` (a yes/no parameter or a formula) for any.
`Family::marks` works them out, for a type's values, as `Mark`s: a `Mark::Line` (an arc as chords of `ARC_STEP` degrees; a
label as a `Mark::Label`, lettered with `font.rs` by `lettering` where it is drawn) or a `Mark::Dot`. A `text` is `{at, height, value, align?}`: capitals `height` mm
tall, `at` the middle of the line, started, centred or ended there (`Align`); `{Parameter Name}` in `value` reads that parameter
(`said_text`: a number as plainly as it reads, a material by its name), an unknown name or an unclosed `{` is refused by
`Family::check`, and the lettered text is at most `MAX_TEXT` characters. `at` is the middle of the line of text vertically, and `align`
sets the horizontal anchor. A `dot` is a `Circle`, drawn solid in ink. Everything
numeric is checked finite and within `MAX_COORD`; a label's height and a dot's radius must be above zero.

`Model::component_marks` places a component's marks (mirrored, then turned and moved) and `Model::opening_marks` an opening's,
and `render::marks` draws them: lines in the category's pen (`BY_CATEGORY`, so Object Styles and Visibility/Graphics apply), dots
as filled discs. Coarse detail leaves them out. A label's anchor is placed with the component (turned, mirrored, moved) but its
letters never are: they are always drawn at 0 degrees in the view, left to right with a horizontal baseline, however the component
stands (the simplest rule; no flipping by quadrant). Symbols are annotation of the component's level: they draw in that level's
plan and its ceiling plan whatever height the component's forms reach (a ceiling light shows its symbols in the floor plan) and
on no other level's; the forms are outlined by the old rule (whole while any of them is between the view's depth and cut plane,
and not in ceiling plans). A component with no forms draws its symbols the same way. IFC export ignores symbols (they are plan notation, not geometry); the Family Editor's Symbols tab lists
all four parts. Library parts: a symbol of any kind has its own id and GUID (`HasPart`, `keep_parts`). A file written with
`text` or `dot` symbols, or symbols on a category other than a door or a window, is read by an older version only with them left
out or refused, so the file format is unchanged.


## Symbol sets

A symbol set (`symbol_set.rs`) is families that are a plan symbol and nothing else, loaded on demand and never part of a new
project: the starter fixtures (`fixtures.rs`) are in every project, and 76 more would crowd every family list. The
`symbol_set {set, names?}` command adds a set's families to the project (the Electrical tab's Symbols > Load AREI Symbols
button runs it); a family the project has by that name stays as it is, so loading twice changes nothing and an edited family is
never overwritten (`loaded` and `kept` in the reply). Each family has one type, `Standard`, no forms, and the symbols of
`crates/core/data/arei-symbols.json`, in the family `symbols` schema (mm, y up, the origin at the symbol's own origin): a
switch is in category `switch`, a socket in `outlet`, a data socket in `dataoutlet`, a light point or luminaire in `lighting`
and everything else (appliances, consumers, sources, domotics, protection) in `generic`, so the Device and Lighting Fixture
tools list their own kinds and the others are placed with the Component tool. They have no connectors, loads or 3D forms: they
are plan symbols only for now, and a family without a connector raises no warning in `inspect`.

The `arei` set is the graphical symbols of Table 2.23 of the AREI/RGIE (FOD Economie, Book 1), redrawn originally. The names
are those printed in its Dutch and French versions (`name_nl`, `name_fr` in the data), the English ones are working names. The
symbols are drawn at about 30 mm per drawing point, so a socket is about 25 cm wide on a plan. `names` (`en`, `nl`, `fr`) picks
the language of the family names; as given none, a French project gets the French wording, a Dutch project the Dutch
and every other language the English.

# Masses

Moved from the root `CLAUDE.md`, word for word: the root keeps the rules and the map, and this file is read when the area is touched.

A mass (`Mass`, category `mass`) is a footprint (`Mass::footprint`: counter-clockwise whichever way `boundary` runs) extruded from
`base_offset` over `level` up to `top_level` or `height`, as a shaft is, with `params`. Given a `top` outline (as many points as
`boundary`, twin for twin, and running the same way round; `Mass::top_ring` has it counter-clockwise like the footprint) it is lofted
straight between the two (`Mass::lofted`: a `top` equal to the footprint is no loft, and the `mass` command drops it; its `lean`
parameter makes `top` by moving the footprint sideways, a sloped mass). `Model::mass_outline(ms, z)` is the cross section at a height,
the footprint, or each corner that far along its way to its twin (`massing::ring_at`), and everything that measures a mass asks it:
floors, the `massfloor` and `mass` schedules, gross floor area, the plan, snaps. The area is a quadratic of the height, so
`Model::mass_volume` is Simpson's rule on three cross sections, exact. `massing::loft_problem` (which `Model::check` and the IFC import
both ask) refuses a top outline that doesn't pair up, runs the other way round, or collapses the cross section at some sixteenth of
the way up. A plan dashes the outline at its cut height where the plane passes through it (`Model::mass_cut_by`); a section outlines
where its line cuts it and never fills it in poché (`section` leaves masses out of `cuts`; a straight one's stretches come from
`view3d::crossings`, a lofted one's lines from `massing::section_lines`, the cut of its skin of triangles, joined end to end); 3D draws
a straight one as a slab and a lofted one as `massing::tris`, a closed skin turned out (two triangles on a side whose twin
edges are parallel, which makes it flat; a side that twists is cut into `massing::STRIPS` strips up its height, so a twisted loft's volume
in 3D and IFC is a percent or two under the exact one, while the areas and volumes the model reports are exact),
see-through by `graphics::MASS_TRANSPARENCY` unless the view's graphics say otherwise (`Look::with` starts a mass's override there, so a
project with masses never takes its plain shortcut). Show Mass (`show_mass`, MH) is `graphics {hide|show: [mass]}` on one view.
`Model::mass_slices` is the levels it crosses, from its base up to, not including, its top, each with how far the mass goes up from
there: `mass_floors` and the rows of the `massfloor` schedule (`schedule::sources`; a `Row` carries the schedule's category, not its
element's) come from it.
What a mass makes remembers it, under reserved names in `params` as phases and paint are held (`massing.rs`; no project or family
parameter may take them, `Model::check` holds each to a real mass and a level or a face of the right kind, `delete` takes off the marks
naming a mass that goes, and a copy or a split piece loses its own). `mass_floors` leaves `Mass Floor`, `{mass, level}`, on its floors,
so a second run finds them by it, gives them the mass's outline at their level (and the type, if one is given), makes none again, lists
as `stale` the ones on levels the mass no longer crosses and deletes those only with `prune`. `wall_by_face`, `floor_by_face` and
`roof_by_face` build their element by running `wall`, `floor` and `roof` with the face's parameters, so those commands' checks stay the
one place, and leave `Mass Face`, `{mass, face}`: an edge number (numbered from the first point, counter-clockwise) for a wall, `"top"`
for a floor or a roof. A wall stands plumb, so only on a face whose top edge is right over its bottom edge (`massing::plumb`); a floor
and a roof lie on the top outline. `update_by_face` (UF; Revit's Update to Face has no default shortcut) rebuilds the geometry of the
ones asked for, a mass's, or all of them (`massing::follow`: a wall's ends, level, offset and height or top level; a floor's or roof's
boundary, level and offset; the type, a roof's slope and the rest stay) and refuses the lot, naming each, when a face is gone. A mass
mirrored in place runs its outline round the other way, so `relocate` renumbers the faces its walls hold (`massing::mirrored`). Nothing
else ties them to the mass, and IFC carries no mark: what comes back from a file is ordinary. `commands::category` reads `mass` and
`masses` as `mass` (it trims every trailing `s`, which would make `ma`). IFC writes a mass as an `IFCBUILDINGELEMENTPROXY` of object type
`Mass`, its footprint swept up; a lofted one is a closed `IFCTRIANGULATEDFACESET` with a `BIMCraft_Mass` property set (`ifc::LOFT`) whose
`Loft` says as JSON how the footprint and the top outline pair up, since a face set doesn't. Import reads those before the proxies that
become components of families, and takes a lofted one only when that set's outlines are the body's bottom and its top; a mass whose
outline changes from base to top with no such set is left out and listed. The desktop's Massing tab has the Mass tool (`Tool::Mass`:
corners clicked, Enter or the first corner again finishes, `finish_mass`), Show Mass (the button is pressed while the view shows
masses) and, for each selected mass, the Model by Face buttons, which run the face commands, and Update to Face; a mass's Properties
hold its levels and offsets and `Top Outline`, its corners as `x, y` parted by `;`, blank for none.
# Phases and design options

Moved from the root `CLAUDE.md`, word for word: the root keeps the rules and the map, and this file is read when the area is touched.

Phases (`Model::phases`, in order) and design options (`Model::option_sets`, `phasing.rs`) are values an element holds among its
`params`, under names no project parameter or family parameter may take (`phasing::CREATED`, `DEMOLISHED`, `OPTION`; `Phase Created` is the first
phase when it has no value, `Design Option` is `set: option`; `open` renames an older file's project parameter of such a name), so `modify`, copies, schedules (`From::Param` in `schedule::OWN`)
and view filters reach them as any other. `phasing::status` says what an element is at a phase's place in the order (new,
existing, demolished, temporary, or not there); a door or window with none of its own follows its wall (`phasing::value`), and
annotation, which holds no params, belongs to a view. A view's `Graphics` hold `phase` (the project's last unless it says),
`phase_filter` (every status by category unless it says; `Model::phase_filters` show each status by category, overridden or
not at all, and `Model::phase_overrides` draw the overridden ones, never hidden or see-through) and `options` (`{set: option}`,
a set's primary unless it says); `Look::of` hides what a phase, a filter or an option leaves out and paints what a filter
overrides, below the view's own overrides. `Session::phase` and `Session::option` are what commands make (`Session::stamp`
gives each new element its `Phase Created` (none for the first phase, but a door or window is named, or it would follow its
wall) and its `Design Option` where it holds none; a copy takes the session's and loses its `Phase Demolished`; `split`, undo,
redo and the commands that replace the project stamp nothing); a refused command leaves them as they were; they
belong to the session, not the model, and the desktop sets them before each command (`BimApp::made_in`): the phase of the view
on screen when it has a phase or a phase filter of its own, and the active design option (`activate`, which shows it in the
view too). What was made in the first phase holds no value, so a phase put in before the first, or the first deleted, names it first
(`phasing::pin_first`; a door or window follows its wall, which is named). Deleting or combining a phase moves what was in it to
`into` (`phasing::move_phase`), and renaming a phase, an option or a set takes the elements, the views and the rules of filters
and schedules along; accepting a set keeps the primary's elements and deletes the rest.
IFC carries them in property sets named `ifc::PHASING`, `BIMCraft_Phasing`. An element that holds a phase or an option gets one:
`Phase Created` (always: the first phase is named too, with `ifc::IMPLIED` as its description where the element holds none, but a
door or window holds only what it says, or one with no phase would stop following its wall), `Phase Demolished` and `Design
Option`, as text. The project gets one when an element holds a phase or an option, or it changed its phases, filters or overrides,
or has an option set: `Phases`, a list of the names in order, and, where it changed them, `Phase Filters`, `Phase Overrides` and
`Design Option Sets` as the JSON a project file holds them in; a project that uses none of it writes none, and the file is as it
was. A phased project also says, for any tool that reads IFC's own words, what the work does to each element: `Status`
(`ifc::ifc_status`) in its `Pset_*Common` (`ifc::common_pset`, the one set that holds `LoadBearing` too), `DEMOLISH` where it is
taken down, `TEMPORARY` where that is in the phase it was made in, `EXISTING` where it was made in the first phase and `NEW`
else; a door or window with no phase says its wall's. It is written, not read: the import still takes phases from `BIMCraft_Phasing`. `import.rs` reads them beside the project parameters: what the project can't have (a phase or an option it hasn't, a
demolition before the creation, a list or a JSON that breaks `phasing::check_project`) is left out and listed, and the element
stays (it is the property, not the element, that breaks the rule); an implied `Phase Created` is no value; no other set is read, so
one another tool writes for phases, `Phasing` say, changes nothing.
A schedule sorts and groups `Phase Created` and `Phase Demolished` by the phase's place in `Model::phases`, not by its name, no
`Phase Demolished` coming after every phase (`schedule::sorts_as`); its filters still compare the names. The desktop's Demolish
tool (DW, `BimApp::demolish`, in the Modify tab's Phasing panel) runs `modify {params: {Phase Demolished}}` on the element clicked in a
plan, a section or the 3D view: the phase of the view on screen (the project's last unless it has one), or null when the element
already comes down in it, one undo step a click. A door or window that only follows its wall gets a note instead, and an element that
holds no `params` (annotation, levels, grids, shafts) says so and changes nothing.
The view control bar's Renovation menu (`BimApp::renovation_menu`, `phasing.rs` in the desktop, the same in both profiles) says in plain
words which phase of the work a plan, a section or the 3D view shows: All (no phase and no phase filter of its own, the view as it
starts), Existing (the project's first phase, every status by its category), Demolition (the last phase through a filter that hides
what is new, draws what stood before by its category and what comes down overridden) and New (the last through one that draws what
stood before overridden and hides what comes down). A pick is one `graphics {phase, phase_filter}`, one undo step. The words map onto
filters by what they do, never by their names, which a project renames or has in its own language (`RENOVATION`, `renovation`,
`filter_for`): the project's `Show Previous + Demolished` and `Show Previous + New` to start with. A choice the project has no
filter for is greyed out and says so, a view whose phase and filter match none of them shows Custom, the menu is greyed out where
a view template sets the phase, and the Sketch scale leaves it out with the rest of phasing.

# Structure and the discipline tabs (Plumbing, Electrical, SPDA, Data)

Moved from the root `CLAUDE.md`, word for word: the root keeps the rules and the map, and this file is read when the area is touched.

Structure (`runs.rs`, `structure.rs`; the design for the five discipline tabs is in [docs/disciplines.md](../disciplines.md)). A run
(`model::Run`) is a straight element from `start` to `end` in plan; its `offset` mm over its level is the height of its `justify` line
(top, centre or bottom) at the start, `end_offset` at the end (level when none), `system` the name of the system it is in: a beam, a
strip footing, a pipe (Plumbing), and what the other tabs draw (conduits, cable trays, down conductors, data cabling) as further
`Element` variants over the same struct, as `Door` and `Window` share `Opening`; `model::run_arm!` is the pattern for any of them, so a
place that treats runs alike names no category, and a new category is a line there. Its type is `Types::runs[category][name]`, a `RunType`
(`width` across by `depth` deep, or round, in a `material` of the library). The section is square to the axis, so a sloped run is
`depth / cos θ` deep vertically (`Geom::half`). `runs::Geom` is the one place that knows the geometry (centre line, `footprint`,
`prism` for a rectangle, `tube` for a round one, `z_span`); plans, sections (a prism is cut like any solid; a tube by the plane
through the section's line, `Solid::cuts`: the hull of where its edges cross it, a ring, an ellipse when oblique), 3D, snaps and IFC call
it and know no category. A run's heights are those of its `justify` line, which a beam or a footing has at the top by default and
anything else at the middle (`runs::default_justify`); the desktop keeps each run tool's own justification and offset
(`keep_run_options`). A beam or strip footing can't stand or lean past 75°
(`runs::check`, `may_stand`: what stands is a column; a pipe, a conduit or a conductor may stand, a riser). In plan (`render::stands`) a footing or a run
hangs under the level it is drawn on, its top flush with the view's bottom, and is seen (`seen_below` allows `TOL` for these only,
or a wall of the storey below would show in the plan above); through the cut plane it's cut; over it and under the view range's top
it's dashed; a faint dashed centre line is drawn where it's seen or overhead, which is also where a click picks it. A structural column and an
isolated footing are `Column`s in their own categories (`Element::StructuralColumn`, `Element::Footing`; ask `Element::column()`,
`Model::column_type(e)` and `column_outline(e)`, which take the element, not the column) with types of their own
(`Types::structural_column`, `Types::footing`); a footing is laid down, its `height` its thickness and its `base_offset` putting its
top at the level (the command's `thickness` and `offset`). A floor is `structural` or not, the one flag, and its schedule and IFC say it.
`runs_of` and `stood_of` build what a command would make, so a tool's sketch is the element its click makes. The desktop's
`Tool::Run(category, start)` and `Tool::Stand(category)` serve every category: a tab adds a ribbon button and its rows in
`structure.rs`, `properties.rs` and `lang.rs`, not a tool. The Floor tool makes structural floors while `floor_structural` is set (SB,
the Structure tab's button; every other `set_tool` clears it); CL is the structural column on the Structure tab and the architectural one
elsewhere, as in Revit. IFC writes a run as an extrusion along its own axis (`Step::body_along`, `aim`) of the class and predefined type
the one table `runs::IFC` gives its category (import reads the same table back, `runs::from_ifc`), each structural element with
`LoadBearing` in its `Pset_*Common`, a run's system as an `IfcSystem` (named for it, its GlobalIds following the name) the runs in it
are assigned to by an `IfcRelAssignsToGroup`, its `Justification` and `Category` in `BIMCraft_Run`, and its material as an `IfcMaterial`. A beam, a column, a structural column and a
pad footing carry their section on their type, the IFC4 way (`Step::typed_member`, `write_types`): the `IfcBeamType`, `IfcColumnType` or
`IfcFootingType` is related by `IfcRelAssociatesMaterial` to an `IfcMaterialProfileSet` of one `IfcMaterialProfile`, holding the type's
material (a beam type's; a column type has none, so the material is `$`) and its profile, an `IfcRectangleProfileDef` of the width by the
depth or an `IfcCircleProfileDef` of half the width, in millimetres as every length is. Each occurrence is related to an
`IfcMaterialProfileSetUsage` of that set (one for each cardinal point, shared by the occurrences placed by it): a beam's cardinal point is
the line its heights are on, the top (8), the middle (5) or the bottom (2) of its section, a column's and a footing's the middle (5). The
beam has no other material association, so the importer reads a run's material through the usage (`element_material`). The profile
definition (`Step::section_profile`, keyed by `Section`) is written once for a section, and the type's profile and its occurrences' bodies
share it; two types of one name and two sections (a column's and a structural column's) are two type objects. A strip footing, a pipe and
the other runs have no profile set, only the plain material.
Import (`import::run_in`) finds a run's axis as the direction its body's points spread furthest in (power iteration on their
covariance), so a beam rolled about its axis comes in as the box round it; an axis that stands (a riser) has its width along east and
runs up; the justification BIMCraft wrote puts the heights back on the line they were typed at (`Geom::half`), none meaning the middle;
a system comes from the IfcSystem the product is assigned to, and its category from the class and type, or BIMCraft's `Category`
where a class has several; `LoadBearing` makes a column or a floor structural.

**Sizing** is a command with no model behind it, so it needs no connectors: `circuit` (`nbr5410.rs`, its tables in `nbr5410/tables.rs` as NBR 5410:2004 prints them: Tabelas 36 and 37 current capacity for methods A1 to D, 40 and 41 temperature and soil, 42 and 45 grouping, 47, 48 and 58) sizes one electrical circuit for copper: the design current from watts or VA, the demand and power factors and the phases at the voltage `system` it is given (it reads nothing from the model), then the smallest section and breaker with I_B ≤ I_n ≤ I_Z (which gives I_2 = 1.45 I_n ≤ 1.45 I_Z for the breakers of NBR NM 60898) and a voltage drop within the limit (4 %, from the conductor's resistance at its working temperature and 0.1 ohm/km), with the neutral and the protective conductor. A section or breaker already chosen is never made smaller. It does not check aluminium, trays (methods E and F), several layers, short circuit, harmonics or the conditions of a reduced neutral, and says so; a circuit in the model and a panel schedule come after it. `conduit_fill` (`conduit.rs`, its catalogues in `conduit/tables.rs`) checks a conduit's fill: the conductors of a circuit (phases, neutral, protective; by outside diameter) over the conduit's inside, at most 53 % for one cable, 31 % for two and 40 % for three or more (NBR 5410), and the smallest size of a family that takes them. The dimensions are the makers' own (Amanco Wavin PVC, Elecon steel, Corfio flexible cable), each family naming its document, page and address; the inside diameter is derived (outside less twice the wall); a cable the catalogue lacks (EPR, above 240 mm²) leaves the fill pending, never guessed. Trays are not sized. `drain_size` and `vent_size` (`drainage.rs`) size sanitary drains and vents as NBR 8160 asks, by the fixture units (UHC) they carry, with the standard's own tables: Tabela 3 (the units and smallest drain of each fixture), 5 (branches), 7 (building drains and collectors by slope), 6 (stacks by the building's floors), 8 (branch vents), 2 (vent stacks and headers by the DN served, its units and the longest length of each vent DN) and 1 (a trap's longest run to its vent). A drain is never smaller than its fixtures' own drains or than one flowing into it (`min_dn`), and a building drain is DN 100 at least. They are stateless, so none of this needs a pipe network; a network that carries the units along the runs comes with connectors. `storm_size` (`storm.rs`) sizes storm drains as NBR 10844 asks: the flow Q = I·A/60 from a rainfall and a roof area, a downpipe by the inner diameter of the standard's Figure 3 abacuses (read curve by curve: the water depth in the gutter, the downpipe's length and a sharp-edged or funnel outlet; 70 mm inside at least; off the chart nothing is read) and a horizontal drain by Manning at two thirds full (n 0.011, which reproduces its Table 4 within 1 %; 0.5 % slope at least). `water_size` (`water.rs`) sizes a cold water pipe of PVC soldável as NBR 5626 asks: the design flow of the fixtures by the method the project chooses (weights, Q = 0.3 √ΣP, or every fixture at once), the smallest DN within 3 m/s, the Darcy-Weisbach head loss over the length and the equivalent length of the fittings, and the pressure left (10 kPa at least at a point of use). `hydrant_size` (`hydrant.rs`) sizes hydrants and hose reels as IT 22/2025 of the CBPMESP asks: the system type and fire reserve of Tabela 3 by occupation column and built area, the flow of the two most unfavourable jets of Tabela 2's type, and a pipe's speed (5 m/s at most), Hazen-Williams head loss (Tabela 1) and the head needed at its start. `load_points` (`loads.rs`) lists what a dwelling's rooms must have as NBR 5410:2004 item 9.5.2 asks: one ceiling lighting point per room (100 VA up to 6 m², 60 VA more for each whole 4 m² above) and the general-use outlets by the room's kind, which its name says or `kind` gives (a bathroom 1; kitchen, pantry, service area and laundry one for each 3.5 m of perimeter; room and bedroom one for each 5 m; veranda 1; the others 1 up to 6 m² and by perimeter above), with their power (600 VA each for the first 3 points of a bathroom, kitchen, pantry, service area or laundry and 100 VA after, or for the first 2 by the alternative where those rooms have more than 6 points together; 100 VA a point elsewhere) on the points a room has. It reads the model's rooms (inside the walls' finish) or the rooms it is given, and changes nothing. It leaves out the exceptions to the lighting point and to a veranda's outlet, where the outlets stand, and the TUE, and says so.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Build cases with the original and compare my export.

usage:
  case.py build NAME            # cases/NAME.txt (a script) -> cases/NAME.bimcraft, cases/NAME.ifc (original)
  case.py cmp NAME [-n LINES]   # convert cases/NAME.bimcraft with mine and the original; diff normalised
  case.py all                   # cmp every case, print SAME/DIFF per case
"""
import os, re, subprocess, sys, difflib, glob, tempfile, shutil
ORIG = '/workspace/executable'
MINE = os.environ.get('MINE', '/workspace/.claude/worktrees/agent-a7aa74e0622ce519f/target/release/bimcraft-cli')
D = '/tmp/ifc-export-agent/cases'

def norm(s):
    s = re.sub(r"'\d{4}-\d\d-\d\dT\d\d:\d\d:\d\d'", "'<TIMESTAMP>'", s)
    gm = {}
    def grep(mo):
        g = mo.group(1)
        if g not in gm: gm[g] = 'GID-%d' % (len(gm)+1)
        return "('" + gm[g] + "'"
    s = re.sub(r"\('([0-9A-Za-z_$]{22})'", grep, s)
    return s

def build(name):
    txt = os.path.join(D, name + '.txt')
    bim = os.path.join(D, name + '.bimcraft')
    ifc = os.path.join(D, name + '.ifc')
    args = [ORIG, 'run']
    if open(txt).read().strip():
        args += ['--script', txt]
    args += ['--save', bim, '--save', ifc]
    p = subprocess.run(args, capture_output=True, text=True)
    if p.returncode != 0:
        print('BUILD FAILED', name, p.stderr.strip()[:2000])
        return False
    return True

def export(exe, bim):
    d = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix='ifcx')
    out = os.path.join(d, 'out.ifc')
    p = subprocess.run([exe, 'convert', bim, out], capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=300)
    s = open(out, encoding='utf-8', errors='replace').read() if os.path.exists(out) else ''
    shutil.rmtree(d)
    return p.returncode, p.stdout, p.stderr, s

def cmp(name, n=40, quiet=False):
    bim = os.path.join(D, name + '.bimcraft')
    if not os.path.exists(bim):
        if not build(name): return False
    a = export(ORIG, bim)
    b = export(MINE, bim)
    x = norm(a[3]).splitlines()
    y = norm(b[3]).splitlines()
    ok = x == y and a[0] == b[0]
    if not ok and not quiet:
        if a[0] != b[0] or a[2] != b[2]:
            print('exit/stderr: orig', a[0], a[2].strip()[:300], '| mine', b[0], b[2].strip()[:300])
        for l in list(difflib.unified_diff(x, y, 'orig', 'mine', lineterm='', n=1))[:n]:
            print(l[:400])
    return ok

if __name__ == '__main__':
    a = sys.argv[1:]
    if a[0] == 'build':
        for nm in a[1:]: build(nm)
    elif a[0] == 'cmp':
        n = 40
        if '-n' in a:
            i = a.index('-n'); n = int(a[i+1]); del a[i:i+2]
        for nm in a[1:]:
            r = cmp(nm, n)
            print(nm, 'SAME' if r else 'DIFF')
    elif a[0] == 'all':
        names = sorted(os.path.basename(f)[:-4] for f in glob.glob(D + '/*.txt'))
        if len(a) > 1: names = [x for x in names if re.search(a[1], x)]
        same = 0
        for nm in names:
            r = cmp(nm, quiet=True)
            same += r
            print('%-30s %s' % (nm, 'SAME' if r else 'DIFF'))
        print(same, '/', len(names))

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Test candidate local-coordinate transforms against the original's wall axis points.
usage: xform.py case.bimcraft case.ifc"""
import json, re, sys, math

def fmt(x):
    s = '%.6f' % x
    s = s.rstrip('0')
    return s

bim = json.load(open(sys.argv[1]))
walls = [e for k, e in sorted(bim['elements'].items()) if e['category'] == 'wall']
ents = {}
for line in open(sys.argv[2]):
    m = re.match(r'#(\d+)=(\w+)\((.*)\);$', line.strip())
    if m: ents[int(m.group(1))] = (m.group(2), m.group(3))
axes = []
for i, (t, a) in sorted(ents.items()):
    if t == 'IFCWALL':
        shape = int(a.split(',')[6][1:])
        reps = [int(x) for x in re.findall(r'#(\d+)', ents[shape][1])]
        ax = reps[1]
        poly = int(re.findall(r'#(\d+)', ents[ax][1])[1])
        pts = [ents[int(x)][1].strip('()') for x in re.findall(r'#(\d+)', ents[poly][1])]
        axes.append(pts)

def norm_recip(dx, dy):
    l = math.sqrt(dx*dx + dy*dy); r = 1.0/l
    return dx*r, dy*r
def norm_div(dx, dy):
    l = math.sqrt(dx*dx + dy*dy)
    return dx/l, dy/l

def cand_sub(o, p, d):
    vx, vy = p[0]-o[0], p[1]-o[1]
    c, s = d
    return vx*c + vy*s, vx*(-s) + vy*c

def cand_affine(o, p, d):
    c, s = d
    # columns x=(c,s), y=(-s,c); glam DMat2 inverse
    det = c*c - (-s)*s
    idt = 1.0/det
    ix = (c*idt, -s*idt)      # (y_axis.y * id, -x_axis.y * id)
    iy = (-(-s)*idt, c*idt)   # (-y_axis.x * id, x_axis.x * id)
    tx = -(ix[0]*o[0] + iy[0]*o[1]); ty = -(ix[1]*o[0] + iy[1]*o[1])
    return ix[0]*p[0] + iy[0]*p[1] + tx, ix[1]*p[0] + iy[1]*p[1] + ty

def cand_affine2(o, p, d):
    # rotation transpose without det, translation applied after
    c, s = d
    tx = -(c*o[0] + s*o[1]); ty = -((-s)*o[0] + c*o[1])
    return c*p[0] + s*p[1] + tx, (-s)*p[0] + c*p[1] + ty

cands = {'sub': cand_sub, 'affine': cand_affine, 'affine2': cand_affine2}
norms = {'recip': norm_recip, 'div': norm_div}
for nn, nf in norms.items():
    for cn, cf in cands.items():
        bad = 0
        for w, ax in zip(walls, axes):
            if w.get('arc'): continue
            o = w['start']; p = w['end']
            d = nf(p[0]-o[0], p[1]-o[1])
            for q, want in zip([o, p], ax):
                x, y = cf(o, q, d)
                got = fmt(x) + ',' + fmt(y)
                if got != want: bad += 1
        print(nn, cn, 'mismatches', bad)

    return vx*c + vy*s, vx*(-s) + vy*c

def cand_affine(o, p, d):
    c, s = d
    # columns x=(c,s), y=(-s,c); glam DMat2 inverse
    det = c*c - (-s)*s
    idt = 1.0/det
    ix = (c*idt, -s*idt)      # (y_axis.y * id, -x_axis.y * id)
    iy = (-(-s)*idt, c*idt)   # (-y_axis.x * id, x_axis.x * id)
    tx = -(ix[0]*o[0] + iy[0]*o[1]); ty = -(ix[1]*o[0] + iy[1]*o[1])
    return ix[0]*p[0] + iy[0]*p[1] + tx, ix[1]*p[0] + iy[1]*p[1] + ty

def cand_affine2(o, p, d):
    # rotation transpose without det, translation applied after
    c, s = d
    tx = -(c*o[0] + s*o[1]); ty = -((-s)*o[0] + c*o[1])
    return c*p[0] + s*p[1] + tx, (-s)*p[0] + c*p[1] + ty

norms = {'recip': norm_recip, 'div': norm_div}

input.prompt:
You are helping reimplement a closed program, `bimcraft-cli` 0.10.0 (the command line of a BIM modeler written in Rust; README at /workspace/README.md), as a new Rust program built only from observed behaviour. I own the IFC export (src/ifc/export*.rs) and am handing you one part of it.

## Hard rules (violating any fails the whole project)
- The original binary is `/workspace/executable` (execute-only). Use it only by running it (args, stdin, files, env). NEVER decompile, disassemble, hexdump, strace/ltrace or read it; never modify or delete it; NEVER run `./compile.sh`.
- No internet; don't look for the program's source anywhere. Rust standard library only (no crates).
- Your code goes only in the files you own (below). If a tiny change elsewhere is unavoidable (a hook line), keep it minimal and list it in your report.
- Scratch scripts (Python is fine) live OUTSIDE the repo, in your own dir `/tmp/ifc-export-families/`. Commit only Rust. Don't write report/notes files into the repo.

## Setup
You work in a git worktree. My branch `worktree-agent-a7aa74e0622ce519f` holds the exporter core. First run `git log --oneline -3`; if commit 4cb9202 ("IFC export: hooks for structure and MEP runs...") is not in your history, run `git merge worktree-agent-a7aa74e0622ce519f`. Build: `cargo build --release` (binary at `<your worktree>/target/release/bimcraft-cli`).

Read first: src/ifc/export.rs (top comment: how an element writer works; `Ex`, the element loop, the tail), export_step.rs (number/string formatting), export_geom.rs (glam-like vectors), export_openings.rs (doors/windows: the family branch calls `family::meshes` and `face_sets`), export_family.rs (parameter values + formula evaluator + a naive prism mesher). Also read the original's own design notes: /workspace/docs/areas/families.md (forms, revolve 32 steps a turn, voids via `csg::subtract` "convex polygons in binary space partitions, built and walked with a worklist rather than recursion", IFC "each form a closed face set, triangles turned out"), /workspace/docs/areas/structure-and-mep.md and /workspace/docs/disciplines.md (the IFC class and predefined type of each family category and `kind`, proxies' object types, connectors → `Pset_ElectricalDeviceCommon` and `BIMCraft_Connector`), and the README rows "Families", "Plumbing", "Electrical", "Lightning protection", "Data", "Files".

## How to test
Build projects with the ORIGINAL and compare both programs' exports. Copy /tmp/ifc-export-agent/tools/case.py (and prof.py, gid.py if useful) into your dir and use it with env `CASES=/tmp/ifc-export-families/cases MINE=<your worktree>/target/release/bimcraft-cli`:
- write a script (one command per line, `cmd {json}`, e.g. `component {"family": "Chair", "at": [1000, 2000], "angle": 30}`) as `$CASES/NAME.txt`; `python3 case.py build NAME` runs the original (`run --script NAME.txt --save NAME.bimcraft --save NAME.ifc`);
- `python3 case.py cmp NAME [-n LINES]` converts NAME.bimcraft with both programs and prints a diff of the normalised IFC (GlobalIds renamed GID-N by first appearance, timestamp normalised) or SAME; `python3 case.py all [regex]` runs all your cases;
- `python3 case.py asset NAME /workspace/assets/test_ifc_export/x.ifc` says whether the ORIGINAL's export of your case equals an expected asset file. The README's Commands table lists every command (`family` creates/changes families with forms, `component` places one); `/workspace/executable commands` prints the catalog; new projects come with ~35 starter families (`families` in the saved .bimcraft).
The hidden tests compare exports exactly on projects like the asset files, so the goal is byte equality after normalisation: entity order, numbering, number formatting, point order, triangle order.

## What's known
- Geometry is glam-style f64: normalize = v * (1/len), len = sqrt(x*x+y*y); numbers are printed {:.6} (directions {:.12}) with trailing zeros cut, a negative zero printed `0.` and tiny negatives `-0.` (so near-zero results' signs are visible: mimic the computation).
- Prism forms (observed in assets): caps triangulated by ear clipping from the first corner ((p3,p0,p1),(p3,p1,p2) for a quad); the cap at `to` first and the cap at `from` reversed, interleaved triangle by triangle; then the sides, edge i→j: (b_i,b_j,t_j),(b_i,t_j,t_i); point list deduplicated in first-use order. Unknown: concave/CW profiles, circles' segment count, xz/yz plane orientation, revolves, voids (CSG output is visibly BSP-split triangles: see the Casement Window's sash in /workspace/assets/test_ifc_export/walls.ifc, entity #516/#517), mirroring, the door/window flips, components' placement.

## YOUR AREA: family forms as meshes, and components
Files you own: src/ifc/export_family.rs (rewrite freely; keep `Mesh`, `Hosted`, `values`, `meshes` usable by export_openings.rs or adapt the call there), src/ifc/export_components.rs (`write_component`, called for each element of category `component` in id order), and in src/ifc/export_openings.rs only the family branch (`Some((_, f)) => {...}`), `face_sets`, and the family-related bits of naming/material association/operation types. I (the core owner) won't touch those; I keep the rest of export_openings.rs (openings, plain types) and export.rs.
1. #!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Test sloped floor z formulas against the original's brep points."""
import json, re, sys, math
def fmt(x):
    s = '%.6f' % (x + 0.0)
    return s.rstrip('0')
bim = json.load(open(sys.argv[1]))
floors = [e for k, e in sorted(bim['elements'].items()) if e['category'] == 'floor']
ents = {}
for line in open(sys.argv[2]):
    m = re.match(r'#(\d+)=(\w+)\((.*)\);$', line.strip())
    if m: ents[int(m.group(1))] = (m.group(2), m.group(3))
breps = []
for i, (t, a) in sorted(ents.items()):
    if t == 'IFCSLAB':
        shape = int(a.split(',')[6][1:])
        rep = int(re.findall(r'#(\d+)', ents[shape][1])[0])
        items = [int(x) for x in re.findall(r'#(\d+)', ents[rep][1])][1:]
        # collect all points of first brep: the 2n points before the first polyloop
        b = items[0]
        shell = int(re.findall(r'#(\d+)', ents[b][1])[0])
        faces = [int(x) for x in re.findall(r'#(\d+)', ents[shell][1])]
        loops = []
        for f in faces:
            fb = int(re.findall(r'#(\d+)', ents[f][1])[0])
            pl = int(re.findall(r'#(\d+)', ents[fb][1])[0])
            loops.append([ents[int(x)][1].strip('()') for x in re.findall(r'#(\d+)', ents[pl][1])])
        breps.append(loops)

def cands(e, p, t):
    s = math.radians(e['slope']); off = e.get('offset', 0.0)
    tail, head = e['arrow']
    dx, dy = head[0]-tail[0], head[1]-tail[1]
    L = math.sqrt(dx*dx+dy*dy); r = 1.0/L; u = (dx*r, dy*r)
    v = (p[0]-tail[0], p[1]-tail[1])
    tn = math.tan(s); cs = math.cos(s); sn = math.sin(s)
    tv = t / cs
    out = {}
    d = v[0]*u[0] + v[1]*u[1]
    out['dot*tan'] = (off + d*tn - tv, off + d*tn)
    out['dot*tan_b2'] = (off + d*tn - t/cs, off + d*tn)
    top = off + d*tn
    out['bot_then_top'] = (top - tv, (top - tv) + tv)
    out['bot_then_top2'] = (top - tv, (top - tv) + t / cs)
    out['tan_dot'] = (off + tn*d - tv, off + tn*d)
    out['sin/cos'] = (off + d*sn/cs - tv, off + d*sn/cs)
    # rise = d * tan, then off + rise
    return out

stats = {}
for e, loops in zip(floors, breps):
    # bottom loop reversed is loops[0], top loop is loops[1]
    t = 200.0
    top = loops[1]; bot = list(reversed(loops[0]))
    ring = e['boundary']
    for k, p in enumerate(ring):
        for name, (zb, zt) in cands(e, p, t).items():
            ok = (fmt(p[0]) + ',' + fmt(p[1]) + ',' + fmt(zt)) == top[k] and (fmt(p[0]) + ',' + fmt(p[1]) + ',' + fmt(zb)) == bot[k]
            stats.setdefault(name, [0, 0])[0 if ok else 1] += 1
for k, v in stats.items(): print(k, 'ok', v[0], 'bad', v[1])

## Hard rules (violating any fails the whole project)
- The original binary is `/workspace/executable` (execute-only). Use it only by running it (args, stdin, files, env). NEVER decompile, disassemble, hexdump, strace/ltrace or read it; never modify or delete it; NEVER run `./compile.sh`.

- Scratch scripts (Python is fine) live OUTSIDE the repo, in your own dir `/tmp/ifc-export-families/`. Commit only Rust. Don't write report/notes files into the repo.

## Setup
You work in a git worktree. My branch `worktree-agent-a7aa74e0622ce519f` holds the exporter core. First run `git log --oneline -3`; if commit 7f18e6d is not in your history, run `git merge worktree-agent-a7aa74e0622ce519f`. Build: `cargo build --release` (binary `<your worktree>/target/release/bimcraft-cli`). Note: the shell sandbox rejects some compound commands (e.g. `cd /tmp/... && python3 - <<EOF`); write scripts to files with your file-writing tool and run them with plain commands.

Read first: src/ifc/export.rs (top comment: how an element writer works; `Ex`, the element loop, the tail), export_step.rs (number/string formatting), export_geom.rs (glam-like vectors), export_openings.rs (doors/windows: the family branch calls `family::meshes` and `face_sets`), export_family.rs (parameter values + formula evaluator + a naive prism mesher with an ear-clipper), export_slabs.rs (`loft_mesh`, `face_set_plain`: a lofted mass's mesh, which already matches the original). Also the original's own design notes: /workspace/docs/areas/families.md (forms, revolve "32 steps to a turn", voids via `csg::subtract` "convex polygons in binary space partitions, built and walked with a worklist rather than recursion", IFC "each form a closed face set, triangles turned out"), /workspace/docs/areas/structure-and-mep.md and /workspace/docs/disciplines.md (IFC class and predefined type of each family category and `kind`, proxies' object types, connectors → `Pset_ElectricalDeviceCommon` and `BIMCraft_Connector`), and the README rows "Families", "Plumbing", "Electrical", "Lightning protection", "Data", "Files".

Build projects with the ORIGINAL and compare both programs' exports. Copy /tmp/ifc-export-agent/tools/case.py into your dir and run it with env `CASES=/tmp/ifc-export-families/cases MINE=<your worktree>/target/release/bimcraft-cli`:

- `python3 case.py cmp NAME [-n LINES]` converts NAME.bimcraft with both programs and prints a diff of the normalised IFC (GlobalIds renamed GID-N by first appearance, timestamp normalised) or SAME; `python3 case.py all [regex]` runs all your cases;
- `python3 case.py asset NAME /workspace/assets/test_ifc_export/x.ifc` says whether the ORIGINAL's export of your case equals an expected asset file. The hidden tests compare exports exactly on projects like the asset files, so the goal is byte equality after normalisation: entity order, numbering, number formatting, point order, triangle order. #!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Search for the original's roof arithmetic: which formula gives the observed signs of the
eave heights on rectangle hip roofs."""
import json, math, re, sys, itertools
meta = json.load(open('/tmp/ifc-export-agent/rf_rects_meta.json'))
# observed: per roof, per face (0..3), sign of the bottom z at the eave points
ents = {}
for line in open('/tmp/ifc-export-agent/cases/rf_rects.ifc'):
    m = re.match(r'#(\d+)=(\w+)\((.*)\);$', line.strip())
    if m: ents[int(m.group(1))] = (m.group(2), m.group(3))
obs = []
cur = []
for i, (t, a) in sorted(ents.items()):
    if t == 'IFCFACETEDBREP':
        shell = int(re.findall(r'#(\d+)', a)[0])
        faces = [int(x) for x in re.findall(r'#(\d+)', ents[shell][1])]
        fb = int(re.findall(r'#(\d+)', ents[faces[1]][1])[0])  # top loop: ring order
        # bottom points: the first n points of the brep are the bottom ring in ring order
        pl = int(re.findall(r'#(\d+)', ents[fb][1])[0])
        top = [int(x) for x in re.findall(r'#(\d+)', ents[pl][1])]
        n = len(top)
        bot = [top[0] - n + k for k in range(n)]
        zs = [ents[b][1].strip('()').split(',')[2] for b in bot]
        cur.append(''.join('-' if z.startswith('-') else '+' for z in zs[:2]))
    if t == 'IFCROOF':
        obs.append(cur); cur = []
def fmt(x):
    s = '%.6f' % (x + 0.0)
    return s.rstrip('0')
def sg(z): return '-' if fmt(z).startswith('-') else '+'
def norm(v):
    l = math.sqrt(v[0]*v[0] + v[1]*v[1]); r = 1.0/l
    return (v[0]*r, v[1]*r)

def faces_of(b, slope, variant):
    A, B, C, D = [tuple(map(float, p)) for p in b]
    tn = math.tan(math.radians(slope))
    pts = [A, B, C, D]
    E = []
    for i in range(4):
        p, q = pts[i], pts[(i + 1) % 4]
        d = norm((q[0]-p[0], q[1]-p[1]))
        E.append((p, d, (-d[1], d[0])))
    # vertex velocities
    vel = []
    for i in range(4):
        (_, d1, n1), (_, d2, n2) = E[(i - 1) % 4], E[i]
        if variant['vel'] == 'solve':
            det = n1[0]*n2[1] - n1[1]*n2[0]
            vx = (1*n2[1] - 1*n1[1]) / det
            vy = (n1[0]*1 - n2[0]*1) / det
            vel.append((vx, vy))
        elif variant['vel'] == 'bisect':
            bx, by = norm((n1[0] + n2[0], n1[1] + n2[1]))
            c = bx*n1[0] + by*n1[1]
            vel.append((bx / c, by / c))
        elif variant['vel'] == 'bisect2':
            bx, by = norm((n1[0] + n2[0], n1[1] + n2[1]))
            c = bx*n1[0] + by*n1[1]
            k = 1.0 / c
            vel.append((bx * k, by * k))
    # events: edge i between vertex i and i+1 collapses when length = 0
    ev = []
    for i in range(4):
        p, d, n = E[i]
        u, v = vel[i], vel[(i + 1) % 4]
        rate = (v[0]-u[0])*d[0] + (v[1]-u[1])*d[1]
        q = pts[(i + 1) % 4]
        L = (q[0]-p[0])*d[0] + (q[1]-p[1])*d[1]
        t = L / -rate if rate < 0 else float('inf')
        ev.append(t)
    w = b[1][0] - b[0][0]; h = b[2][1] - b[1][1]
    # rectangle: the short edges collapse first; nodes from the vertices' moves
    nodes = {}
    for i in range(4):
        t = ev[i]
        if t == float('inf'): continue
        p = pts[i]; v = vel[i]
        if variant['node'] == 'move':
            nodes[i] = ((p[0] + v[0]*t, p[1] + v[1]*t), t)
        else:
            nodes[i] = ((p[0] + t * v[0], p[1] + t * v[1]), t)
    return pts, E, vel, ev, nodes, tn

def zfun(variant, E, i, node, tn, p):
    a, d, n = E[i]
    (nx, ny), t = node
    zn = t * tn
    if variant['z'] == 'node_dot':
        return zn + ((p[0]-nx)*n[0] + (p[1]-ny)*n[1]) * tn
    if variant['z'] == 'node_dot2':
        return zn - ((nx-p[0])*n[0] + (ny-p[1])*n[1]) * tn
    if variant['z'] == 'grad':
        gx, gy = n[0]*tn, n[1]*tn
        c0 = zn - (gx*nx + gy*ny)
        return gx*p[0] + gy*p[1] + c0
    if variant['z'] == 'edge':
        return ((p[0]-a[0])*n[0] + (p[1]-a[1])*n[1]) * tn
    return 0.0

variants = []
for vv in ['solve', 'bisect', 'bisect2']:
    for nn in ['move']:
        for zz in ['node_dot', 'node_dot2', 'grad', 'edge']:
            for which in ['first', 'last', 'max', 'min']:
                variants.append({'vel': vv, 'node': nn, 'z': zz, 'which': which})
for var in variants:
    ok = 0; tot = 0
    for (b, s), o in zip(meta, obs):
        pts, E, vel, ev, nodes, tn = faces_of(b, s, var)
        w = b[1][0] - b[0][0]; h = b[2][1] - b[1][1]
        # face nodes: for a rectangle w>h: ridge nodes are where the short edges (1 and 3) collapse
        short = [1, 3] if h < w else [0, 2]
        ridge = [nodes[k] for k in short]
        for f in range(4):
            cand = ridge if var['which'] in ('first', 'last') else ridge
            node = ridge[0] if var['which'] == 'first' else ridge[1] if var['which'] == 'last' else (max if var['which']=='max' else min)(ridge, key=lambda r: r[1])
            p0 = pts[f]; p1 = pts[(f + 1) % 4]
            got = sg(zfun(var, E, f, node, tn, p0)) + sg(zfun(var, E, f, node, tn, p1))
            ok += got == o[f]; tot += 1
    print(var, ok, tot)

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Search for the original's roof arithmetic: which formula gives the observed signs of the
eave heights on rectangle hip roofs."""
import json, math, re, sys, itertools
meta = json.load(open('/tmp/ifc-export-agent/rf_rects_meta.json'))
# observed: per roof, per face (0..3), sign of the bottom z at the eave points
ents = {}
for line in open('/tmp/ifc-export-agent/cases/rf_rects.ifc'):
    m = re.match(r'#(\d+)=(\w+)\((.*)\);$', line.strip())
    if m: ents[int(m.group(1))] = (m.group(2), m.group(3))
obs = []
cur = []
for i, (t, a) in sorted(ents.items()):
    if t == 'IFCFACETEDBREP':
        shell = int(re.findall(r'#(\d+)', a)[0])
        faces = [int(x) for x in re.findall(r'#(\d+)', ents[shell][1])]
        fb = int(re.findall(r'#(\d+)', ents[faces[1]][1])[0])  # top loop: ring order
        # bottom points: the first n points of the brep are the bottom ring in ring order
        pl = int(re.findall(r'#(\d+)', ents[fb][1])[0])
        top = [int(x) for x in re.findall(r'#(\d+)', ents[pl][1])]
        n = len(top)
        bot = [top[0] - n + k for k in range(n)]
        zs = [ents[b][1].strip('()').split(',')[2] for b in bot]
        cur.append(''.join('-' if z.startswith('-') else '+' for z in zs[:2]))
    if t == 'IFCROOF':
        obs.append(cur); cur = []
def fmt(x):
    s = '%.6f' % (x + 0.0)
    return s.rstrip('0')
def sg(z): return '-' if fmt(z).startswith('-') else '+'
def norm(v):
    l = math.sqrt(v[0]*v[0] + v[1]*v[1]); r = 1.0/l
    return (v[0]*r, v[1]*r)

def faces_of(b, slope, variant):
    A, B, C, D = [tuple(map(float, p)) for p in b]
    tn = math.tan(math.radians(slope))
    pts = [A, B, C, D]
    E = []
    for i in range(4):
        p, q = pts[i], pts[(i + 1) % 4]
        d = norm((q[0]-p[0], q[1]-p[1]))
        E.append((p, d, (-d[1], d[0])))
    # vertex velocities
    vel = []
    for i in range(4):
        (_, d1, n1), (_, d2, n2) = E[(i - 1) % 4], E[i]
        if variant['vel'] == 'solve':
            det = n1[0]*n2[1] - n1[1]*n2[0]
            vx = (1*n2[1] - 1*n1[1]) / det
            vy = (n1[0]*1 - n2[0]*1) / det
            vel.append((vx, vy))
        elif variant['vel'] == 'bisect':
            bx, by = norm((n1[0] + n2[0], n1[1] + n2[1]))
            c = bx*n1[0] + by*n1[1]
            vel.append((bx / c, by / c))
        elif variant['vel'] == 'bisect2':
            bx, by = norm((n1[0] + n2[0], n1[1] + n2[1]))
            c = bx*n1[0] + by*n1[1]
            k = 1.0 / c
            vel.append((bx * k, by * k))
    # events: edge i between vertex i and i+1 collapses when length = 0
    ev = []
    for i in range(4):
        p, d, n = E[i]
        u, v = vel[i], vel[(i + 1) % 4]
        rate = (v[0]-u[0])*d[0] + (v[1]-u[1])*d[1]
        q = pts[(i + 1) % 4]
        L = (q[0]-p[0])*d[0] + (q[1]-p[1])*d[1]
        t = L / -rate if rate < 0 else float('inf')
        ev.append(t)
    w = b[1][0] - b[0][0]; h = b[2][1] - b[1][1]
    # rectangle: the short edges collapse first; nodes from the vertices' moves
    nodes = {}
    for i in range(4):
        t = ev[i]
        if t == float('inf'): continue
        p = pts[i]; v = vel[i]
        if variant['node'] == 'move':
            nodes[i] = ((p[0] + v[0]*t, p[1] + v[1]*t), t)
        else:
            nodes[i] = ((p[0] + t * v[0], p[1] + t * v[1]), t)
    return pts, E, vel, ev, nodes, tn

def zfun(variant, E, i, node, tn, p):
    a, d, n = E[i]
    (nx, ny), t = node
    zn = t * tn
    if variant['z'] == 'node_dot':
        return zn + ((p[0]-nx)*n[0] + (p[1]-ny)*n[1]) * tn
    if variant['z'] == 'node_dot2':
        return zn - ((nx-p[0])*n[0] + (ny-p[1])*n[1]) * tn
    if variant['z'] == 'grad':
        gx, gy = n[0]*tn, n[1]*tn
        c0 = zn - (gx*nx + gy*ny)
        return gx*p[0] + gy*p[1] + c0
    if variant['z'] == 'edge':
        return ((p[0]-a[0])*n[0] + (p[1]-a[1])*n[1]) * tn
    return 0.0

variants = []
for vv in ['solve', 'bisect', 'bisect2']:
    for nn in ['move']:
        for zz in ['node_dot', 'node_dot2', 'grad', 'edge']:
            for which in ['first', 'last', 'max', 'min']:
                variants.append({'vel': vv, 'node': nn, 'z': zz, 'which': which})
for var in variants:
    ok = 0; tot = 0
    for (b, s), o in zip(meta, obs):
        pts, E, vel, ev, nodes, tn = faces_of(b, s, var)
        w = b[1][0] - b[0][0]; h = b[2][1] - b[1][1]
        # face nodes: for a rectangle w>h: ridge nodes are where the short edges (1 and 3) collapse
        short = [1, 3] if h < w else [0, 2]
        ridge = [nodes[k] for k in short]
        for f in range(4):
            cand = ridge if var['which'] in ('first', 'last') else ridge
            node = ridge[0] if var['which'] == 'first' else ridge[1] if var['which'] == 'last' else (max if var['which']=='max' else min)(ridge, key=lambda r: r[1])
            p0 = pts[f]; p1 = pts[(f + 1) % 4]
            got = sg(zfun(var, E, f, node, tn, p0)) + sg(zfun(var, E, f, node, tn, p1))
            ok += got == o[f]; tot += 1
    print(var, ok, tot)

1	//! The straight skeleton of a roof's footprint: its outline counter-clockwise and its
2	//! courtyards clockwise, the roof to the left of every edge, each edge moving in at a speed of
3	//! its own (a gable's 0). Each edge's face is the ring it sweeps: its start, its end, and the
4	//! skeleton's nodes back, each with the time the wavefront reached it.
5	
6	use super::geom::*;
7	
8	const EPS: f64 = 1e-9;
9	
10	#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug)]
11	struct Edge {
12	    a: V2,
13	    d: V2,
14	    n: V2,
15	    w: f64,
16	}
17	
18	#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug)]
19	struct Vert {
20	    p: V2,
21	    t0: f64,
22	    vel: V2,
23	    el: usize,
24	    er: usize,
25	    prev: usize,
26	    next: usize,
27	    alive: bool,
28	    node: usize,
29	}
30	
31	impl Vert {
32	    fn at(&self, t: f64) -> V2 {
33	        self.p + self.vel * (t - self.t0)
34	    }
35	}
36	
37	#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug)]
38	pub struct Node {
39	    pub p: V2,
40	    pub t: f64,
41	}
42	
43	/// An arc of the skeleton: from one node to another, between the faces of two edges (the
44	/// wavefront vertex's incoming and outgoing edges).
45	#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug)]
46	struct Arc {
47	    from: usize,
48	    to: usize,
49	    el: usize,
50	    er: usize,
51	}

53	/// The node at a point, made the first time the wavefront reaches it.
54	fn node_at(nodes: &mut Vec<Node>, p: V2, t: f64) -> usize {
55	    for (i, n) in nodes.iter().enumerate() {
56	        if n.t > 0.0 && n.p.distance(p) < 1e-6 {
57	            return i;
58	        }
59	    }
60	    nodes.push(Node { p, t });
61	    nodes.len() - 1
62	}
63	
64	fn velocity(e1: &Edge, e2: &Edge) -> V2 {
65	    // v·n1 = w1, v·n2 = w2
66	    let det = e1.n.x * e2.n.y - e1.n.y * e2.n.x;
67	    if det.abs() < 1e-12 {
68	        // parallel edges: straight on
69	        let w = if e1.w > e2.w { e1.w } else { e2.w };
70	        return e1.n * w;
71	    }
72	    let x = (e1.w * e2.n.y - e2.w * e1.n.y) / det;
73	    let y = (e1.n.x * e2.w - e2.n.x * e1.w) / det;
74	    v2(x, y)
75	}
76	
77	/// Each edge's face, numbered as the edges are (each ring's edge i from its point i to the
78	/// next, the rings in turn); none for an edge that doesn't move (a gable).
79	pub fn faces(rings: &[Vec<V2>], speeds: &[f64]) -> Vec<Option<Vec<Node>>> {
80	    let mut edges: Vec<Edge> = Vec::new();
81	    let mut nodes: Vec<Node> = Vec::new();
82	    let mut verts: Vec<Vert> = Vec::new();
83	    let mut edge_start: Vec<usize> = Vec::new();
84	    let mut edge_end: Vec<usize> = Vec::new();
85	    for ring in rings {
86	        let n = ring.len();
87	        let base = edges.len();
88	        for i in 0..n {
89	            let a = ring[i];
90	            let b = ring[(i + 1) % n];
91	            let d = (b - a).normalize();
92	            let w = speeds.get(base + i).copied().unwrap_or(1.0);
93	            edges.push(Edge { a, d, n: d.perp(), w });
94	        }
95	        let vbase = verts.len();
96	        for i in 0..n {
97	            let el = base + (i + n - 1) % n;
98	            let er = base + i;
99	            let node = nodes.len();
100	            nodes.push(Node { p: ring[i], t: 0.0 });
101	            verts.push(Vert {
102	                p: ring[i],
103	                t0: 0.0,
104	                vel: velocity(&edges[el], &edges[er]),
105	                el,
106	                er,
107	                prev: vbase + (i + n - 1) % n,
108	                next: vbase + (i + 1) % n,
109	                alive: true,
110	                node,
111	            });
112	        }
113	        for i in 0..n {
114	            edge_start.push(vbase + i);
115	            edge_end.push(vbase + (i + 1) % n);
116	        }
117	    }
118	    let ne = edges.len();
119	    let mut arcs: Vec<Arc> = Vec::new();
120	    let mut t_now = 0.0f64;
121	    let mut guard = 0;
122	    loop {
123	        guard += 1;
124	        if guard > 10000 {
125	            break;
126	        }
127	        // the next event: an edge of the wavefront shrinking away, or a reflex vertex
128	        // reaching an edge it doesn't bound
129	        let mut best: Option<(f64, usize, Option<usize>)> = None;
130	        for (i, v) in verts.iter().enumerate() {
131	            if !v.alive {
132	                continue;
133	            }
134	            let u = &verts[v.next];
135	            let e = &edges[v.er];
136	            let rate = (u.vel - v.vel).dot(e.d);
137	            if rate < -EPS {
138	                let len = (u.at(t_now) - v.at(t_now)).dot(e.d);
139	                let t = t_now + len / (-rate);
140	                if t >= t_now - 1e-9 && best.map(|b| t < b.0 - 1e-9).unwrap_or(true) {
141	                    best = Some((t.max(t_now), i, None));
142	                }
143	            }
144	        }
145	        for (i, v) in verts.iter().enumerate() {
146	            if !v.alive {
147	                continue;
148	            }
149	            let din = edges[v.el].d;
150	            let dout = edges[v.er].d;
151	            if din.cross(dout) >= -EPS {
152	                continue;
153	            }
154	            for (j, a) in verts.iter().enumerate() {
155	                if !a.alive || j == i || a.next == i {
156	                    continue;
157	                }
158	                let f = &edges[a.er];
159	                if a.er == v.el || a.er == v.er {
160	                    continue;
161	                }
162	                let den = f.w - v.vel.dot(f.n);
163	                if den <= EPS {
164	                    continue;
165	                }
166	                let t = ((v.at(t_now) - f.a).dot(f.n) - f.w * t_now) / den + t_now;
167	                if t < t_now - 1e-9 {
168	                    continue;
169	                }
170	                let x = v.at(t);
171	                let b = &verts[a.next];
172	                let sa = (x - a.at(t)).dot(f.d);
173	                let sb = (b.at(t) - x).dot(f.d);
174	                if sa < -1e-7 || sb < -1e-7 {
175	                    continue;
176	                }
177	                if best.map(|bb| t < bb.0 - 1e-9).unwrap_or(true) {
178	                    best = Some((t.max(t_now), i, Some(j)));
179	                }
180	            }
181	        }
182	        let Some((t, i, split)) = best else { break };
183	        t_now = t;
184	        match split {
185	            None => {
186	                // edge event: vertex i and its next meet
187	                let j = verts[i].next;
188	                let x = verts[i].at(t);
189	                let node = node_at(&mut nodes, x, t);
190	                // every other vertex of this wavefront at the same point meets there too
191	                let mut group = vec![i, j];
192	                loop {
193	                    let first = group[0];
194	                    let pv = verts[first].prev;
195	                    if group.contains(&pv) {
196	                        break;
197	                    }
198	                    if verts[pv].at(t).distance(x) < 1e-6 {
199	                        group.insert(0, pv);
200	                    } else {
201	                        break;
202	                    }
203	                }
204	                loop {
205	                    let last = *group.last().unwrap();
206	                    let nv = verts[last].next;
207	                    if group.contains(&nv) {
208	                        break;
209	                    }
210	                    if verts[nv].at(t).distance(x) < 1e-6 {
211	                        group.push(nv);
212	                    } else {
213	                        break;
214	                    }
215	                }
216	                for &g in &group {
217	                    arcs.push(Arc { from: verts[g].node, to: node, el: verts[g].el, er: verts[g].er });
218	                    verts[g].alive = false;
219	                }
220	                let first = group[0];
221	                let last = *group.last().unwrap();
222	                let pv = verts[first].prev;
223	                let nv = verts[last].next;
224	                if pv == last || group.len() >= 3 && verts[last].next == first {
225	                    // the whole wavefront closed at this point
226	                    continue;
227	                }
228	                if pv == nv {
229	                    // two vertices left: they are the ends of a ridge
230	                    let o = pv;
231	                    arcs.push(Arc { from: verts[o].node, to: node, el: verts[o].el, er: verts[o].er });
232	                    verts[o].alive = false;
233	                    continue;
234	                }
235	                let el = verts[first].el;
236	                let er = verts[last].er;
237	                let k = verts.len();
238	                verts.push(Vert {
239	                    p: x,
240	                    t0: t,
241	                    vel: velocity(&edges[el], &edges[er]),
242	                    el,
243	                    er,
244	                    prev: pv,
245	                    next: nv,
246	                    alive: true,
247	                    node,
248	                });
249	                verts[pv].next = k;
250	                verts[nv].prev = k;
251	            }
252	            Some(j) => {
253	                // split event: vertex i reaches the edge from j to its next
254	                let x = verts[i].at(t);
255	                let node = node_at(&mut nodes, x, t);
256	                let v = verts[i];
257	                arcs.push(Arc { from: v.node, to: node, el: v.el, er: v.er });
258	                verts[i].alive = false;
259	                let a = j;
260	                let b = verts[a].next;
261	                let f = verts[a].er;
262	                // one wavefront: from v's prev to x (edges v.el, f), on to b
263	                let k1 = verts.len();
264	                verts.push(Vert { p: x, t0: t, vel: velocity(&edges[v.el], &edges[f]), el: v.el, er: f, prev: v.prev, next: b, alive: true, node });
265	                let k2 = verts.len();
266	                verts.push(Vert { p: x, t0: t, vel: velocity(&edges[f], &edges[v.er]), el: f, er: v.er, prev: a, next: v.next, alive: true, node });
267	                verts[v.prev].next = k1;
268	                verts[b].prev = k1;
269	                verts[a].next = k2;
270	                verts[v.next].prev = k2;
271	                for k in [k1, k2] {
272	                    // a wavefront of two vertices is a ridge
273	                    let p = verts[k].prev;
274	                    if verts[p].prev == k && verts[k].alive {
275	                        arcs.push(Arc { from: verts[p].node, to: verts[k].node, el: verts[p].el, er: verts[p].er });
276	                        verts[p].alive = false;
277	                        verts[k].alive = false;
278	                    }
279	                }
280	            }
281	        }
282	    }
283	    // each edge's face: its start, its end, then the arcs round back to its start
284	    let mut out = Vec::with_capacity(ne);
285	    for e in 0..ne {
286	        if edges[e].w <= EPS {
287	            out.push(None);
288	            continue;
289	        }
290	        let a = verts[edge_start[e]].node;
291	        let b = verts[edge_end[e]].node;
292	        let mut ring = vec![a, b];
293	        let mut cur = b;
294	        let mut used = vec![false; arcs.len()];
295	        let mut ok = false;
296	        for _ in 0..arcs.len() + 2 {
297	            if cur == a {
298	                ok = true;
299	                break;
300	            }
301	            // leave cur along an arc with this face on its right going out (el == e, from cur)
302	            // or one on its left coming in (er == e, to cur)
303	            let mut next = None;
304	            for (k, arc) in arcs.iter().enumerate() {
305	                if used[k] {
306	                    continue;
307	                }
308	                if arc.el == e && arc.from == cur {
309	                    next = Some((k, arc.to));
310	                    break;
311	                }
312	                if arc.er == e && arc.to == cur {
313	                    next = Some((k, arc.from));
314	                    break;
315	                }
316	            }
317	            let Some((k, nn)) = next else { break };
318	            used[k] = true;
319	            if nn == a {
320	                ok = true;
321	                break;
322	            }
323	            ring.push(nn);
324	            cur = nn;
325	        }
326	        if !ok {
327	            out.push(None);
328	            continue;
329	        }
330	        let mut face: Vec<Node> = Vec::new();
331	        for k in &ring {
332	            let n = nodes[*k];
333	            if face.last().map(|l| l.p.distance(n.p) < 1e-6).unwrap_or(false) {
334	                continue;
335	            }
336	            face.push(n);
337	        }
338	        while face.len() > 1 && face[0].p.distance(face[face.len() - 1].p) < 1e-6 {
339	            face.pop();
340	        }
341	        out.push(Some(face));
342	    }
343	    out
344	}

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final message is returned to you as the tool result; it is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- A previously spawned agent cannot be continued from here; every Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).

If omitted, uses the agent definition's model, else the default (inherits from the parent unless a default subagent model is configured).
